title: URL Shortener
objectives: Scope URL Shortener: create short link from long url, redirect short link to original
Size it: 100M redirects/day, about 5,800/s at peak
Defend the design: generate ids with a counter/snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5t ids)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 75 · URL Shortener: A short-link service for SMS links sent by Indian banks and shopping apps, where a 160-character SMS cannot fit a long tracking URL. In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 75 non-functionals: Redirect p99 < 50 ms. 100:1 read/write. Links never collide. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 75 reference path: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids). → Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. → Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 75 risks: Id generation: Hashing the long URL and truncating causes collisions that need retries; a counter or Snowflake id encoded in base62 never collides. 301 versus 302: 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics and makes link edits sticky; 302 keeps every click visible.

cards.body: Boss 75 close: peak QPS for URL Shortener, required components client, lb, service, cache, nosql, and one mitigation.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener: assume 50M daily users each doing about 2 redirects a day, with traffic peaking at 5× the daily average. Estimate peak redirects per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “Create short link from long URL” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Raise the client timeout so retries never happen
Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for URL Shortener jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does URL Shortener need for reliability?

choices.label: Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails
Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low
Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids).

questions.explanation: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids). Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links. The others are tempting but wrong: one big server is still a single point of failure, tight retry loops amplify an outage, and acknowledging before a durable write loses data on a crash.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener must create short link from long URL while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

rationaleOptions.label: User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
A queue removes the need to watch backlog
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request
A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.

title: Pastebin
objectives: Scope Pastebin: create a paste, read a paste by id
Size it: 15M reads/day, about 520/s at peak
Defend the design: metadata in sql, content in object storage

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 76 · Pastebin: Share code snippets and logs between developers, with expiry, like Pastebin or a GitHub gist. In scope: Create a paste; Read a paste by ID; Expire pastes.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 76 non-functionals: Reads p99 < 100 ms. Durable storage. Read-heavy. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 76 reference path: Metadata in SQL, content in object storage. → Cache popular pastes; CDN for raw views. → TTL cleanup worker deletes expired pastes.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 76 risks: Content in the database or object storage?: Small pastes could live in SQL, but object storage keeps the database small, makes backups fast and lets a CDN serve public pastes directly; metadata stays in SQL for queries by owner and expiry. Unguessable ids: Sequential ids let anyone scrape private pastes; random ids from a large space (62 to the power 8 ≈ 218 trillion) make guessing impractical.

title: Rate Limiter
objectives: Scope Rate Limiter: limit requests per user/ip/key, return 429 with retry hint
Size it: 400M API calls/day, about 23,000/s at peak
Defend the design: gateway calls a rate limiter backed by redis token buckets (lua for atomicity)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 77 · Rate Limiter: Protect the OTP and login APIs of a fintech from abuse, shared across every API server. In scope: Limit requests per user/IP/key; Return 429 with retry hint; Configurable rules.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 77 non-functionals: Adds < 5 ms latency. Highly available. Shared across instances. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 77 reference path: Gateway calls a rate limiter backed by Redis token buckets (Lua for atomicity). → Rules stored in SQL and cached locally. → Fail-open for non-critical APIs, fail-closed for OTP.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 77 risks: Fail open or fail closed?: Failing closed during a Redis outage blocks every login; failing open lets attackers through. Choosing keys: Indian mobile carriers put many users behind shared IPs, so per-phone and per-user limits are primary and IP limits are loose, catching only obvious floods.

cards.body: Boss 77 close: peak QPS for Rate Limiter, required components client, lb, service, cache, sql, and one mitigation.

cards.title: The brief

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: Reference sketch

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: The brief

cards.title: Failure modes

title: Uber/Ola
objectives: Scope Uber/Ola: request a ride, match nearby driver
Size it: 80M ride requests/day, about 3,700/s at peak
Defend the design: drivers stream locations via websocket into a geo index (geohash in redis)

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 88 · Uber/Ola: Uber or Ola: match riders with nearby drivers in Indian cities and track trips live. In scope: Request a ride; Match nearby driver; Live location tracking.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 88 non-functionals: Match < 5 s. Location updates every 4 s. No double assignment. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 88 reference path: Drivers stream locations via WebSocket into a geo index (geohash in Redis). → Matching service queries nearby drivers and locks one with CAS. → Trips in SQL; surge via stream processing.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 88 risks: No double assignment: A conditional update on the ride row, or a compare-and-set on the driver's status, guarantees one winner even if two acceptances arrive together. Hot zones: Airports and stations at peak overload a few cells; finer cells and per-zone dispatch partitions keep queries fast.

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 92 · Payment System UPI-style: A UPI-style payment app (PSP) on top of NPCI: pay to a VPA, collect requests and history. In scope: Send money via VPA; Collect requests; Transaction history.

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: Failure modes

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 94 · BookMyShow: BookMyShow: view shows and seat maps, hold seats for 10 minutes, then pay and confirm. In scope: View shows & seat map; Hold seats for 10 min; Pay and confirm.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 94 non-functionals: No double booking. Spikes on blockbuster releases. Fair queueing. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 94 reference path: Seat holds via conditional update or short Redis lock with TTL. → Payment saga releases hold on failure/timeout. → Virtual waiting room queue for blockbuster drops.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 94 risks: Double booking: Because the hold only succeeds when the seat is FREE in the same statement, two users clicking the same seat cannot both succeed. Payment after hold expiry: If a payment succeeds after the hold expired and someone else booked the seat, the system must refund automatically; this is why the hold time exceeds typical payment time.

title: Leaderboard
objectives: Scope Leaderboard: update scores live, show rank and top-n
Size it: 400M score reads/day, about 37,000/s at peak
Defend the design: score events streamed; workers update redis sorted sets per contest

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 96 · Leaderboard: Live fantasy-contest leaderboards during IPL matches: update scores, show rank and top N. In scope: Update scores live; Show rank and top-N; Millions per contest.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 96 non-functionals: Updates within seconds. Massive spikes at match time. Accurate final ranks. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 96 reference path: Score events streamed; workers update Redis sorted sets per contest. → Sharded sorted sets for huge contests; top-N cached. → Final ranks computed in batch for payouts.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 96 risks: Update fan-out: One wicket changes points for every team containing that bowler, possibly millions of teams; recomputing per team in batches every few seconds is cheaper than per ball per team in real time. Accurate final ranks: Live ranks can be approximate, but prize distribution uses a deterministic batch computation with tie-break rules, audited before payout.

rationaleOptions.label: User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 98 · Web Crawler: A web crawler for Indian news and e-commerce sites feeding a search engine. In scope: Fetch pages from seed URLs; Extract and enqueue links; Respect robots.txt and politeness.

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: Reference sketch

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 98 risks: Politeness: Partitioning the frontier by host and assigning each host to one queue enforces per-host rate limits and avoids accidentally overloading small sites. objectives: Scope Proximity Service Yelp: search places nearby, view details
Size it: 250M nearby searches/day, about 12,000/s at peak
Defend the design: geohash/quadtree index cached in memory

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 104 · Proximity Service Yelp: A Yelp-style proximity service: find nearby restaurants or shops, view details, add or update places. In scope: Search places nearby; View details; Add/update places.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 104 non-functionals: Read-heavy. Results < 200 ms. Updates within hours. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 104 reference path: Geohash/quadtree index cached in memory. → Places in SQL with read replicas. → Batch rebuild of geo index.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 104 risks: Geohash or quadtree: Geohash is simple and works in any key-value store; a quadtree adapts cell size to density, which helps in crowded city centres. Update freshness: Places change rarely, so rebuilding or patching the index every few minutes is enough; real-time updates are not required.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “Search places nearby” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate
Raise the client timeout so retries never happen

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for Proximity Service Yelp jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does Proximity Service Yelp need for reliability?

choices.label: Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails
Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Geohash/quadtree index cached in memory.
Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low

questions.explanation: Geohash/quadtree index cached in memory. Places in SQL with read replicas. Batch rebuild of geo index. The others are tempting but wrong: one big server is still a single point of failure, tight retry loops amplify an outage, and acknowledging before a durable write loses data on a crash.

questions.prompt: Proximity Service Yelp must search places nearby while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

rationaleOptions.label: A queue removes the need to watch backlog
A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency
User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.

title: Flash Sale Big Billion Day
objectives: Scope Flash Sale Big Billion Day: show sale item, buy within limit
Size it: 500M buy attempts/day, about 120,000/s at peak
Defend the design: static pages on cdn; waiting room + rate limiting

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 105 · Flash Sale Big Billion Day: A flash sale like Big Billion Days: sell limited stock at a fixed time without overselling. In scope: Show sale item; Buy within limit; Pay.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 105 non-functionals: Massive spike. No overselling. Fairness. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 105 reference path: Static pages on CDN; waiting room + rate limiting. → Stock counter decremented atomically in Redis, persisted to SQL. → Order queue processed by workers.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 105 risks: No overselling: The decrement and the check that stock is above zero happen in one atomic operation; the order is created only after a successful decrement. Fairness: A queue with tokens rewards arrival order; per-account limits and bot detection stop scripts from taking most units.

objectives: Scope Hotel Booking Airbnb/OYO: search hotels, reserve room

Defend the design: search cluster with availability cache

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 106 · Hotel Booking Airbnb/OYO: Hotel booking like Airbnb or OYO: search, reserve a room for dates, pay and confirm. In scope: Search hotels; Reserve room; Pay & confirm.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 106 non-functionals: No double booking. Search < 500 ms. Supplier integrations. Out of scope: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 106 reference path: Search cluster with availability cache. → Booking saga with supplier hold + payment. → Inventory updates via queue.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 106 risks: Multi-night atomicity: A three-night stay must reserve all three nights or none; one transaction with conditional updates on each date row guarantees that. Supplier integrations: External hotels may confirm slowly or fail; a saga with timeouts and automatic cancellation and refund keeps users informed.

title: Stock Exchange Matching
objectives: Scope Stock Exchange Matching: place limit and market orders, match buy and sell orders by price-time priority
Size it: 500M orders/day, about 58,000/s at peak
Defend the design: one single-threaded matching engine per symbol for deterministic order

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 108 · Stock Exchange Matching: A stock-exchange matching engine: accept orders, match by price-time priority, publish trades. In scope: Place limit and market orders; Match buy and sell orders by price-time priority; Publish trades and order book updates.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 108 non-functionals: Matching latency in microseconds to low milliseconds. Deterministic, auditable ordering. No lost or duplicated orders. Out of scope: Portfolio analytics; KYC onboarding.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 108 reference path: One single-threaded matching engine per symbol for deterministic order. → Every order sequenced and journaled before matching. → Hot standby replays the journal on failover.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 108 risks: Determinism: A single thread per symbol and a sequenced input log mean replaying the log always reproduces the same trades, which is what makes audit and failover possible. Latency: Avoiding locks, network hops and garbage-collection pauses in the matching path keeps latency in microseconds; persistence is the replicated log, not a database write per order.

title: S3-like Object Storage
objectives: Scope S3-like Object Storage: put and get objects by bucket and key, store objects from bytes to terabytes
Size it: 2B object requests/day, about 69,000/s at peak
Defend the design: metadata store separate from data nodes

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 113 · S3-like Object Storage: An S3-like object store: PUT and GET objects by bucket and key, list by prefix, eleven nines durability. In scope: PUT and GET objects by bucket and key; Store objects from bytes to terabytes; List objects by prefix.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 113 non-functionals: Eleven nines durability. High availability for reads. Scale to trillions of objects. Out of scope: POSIX file locking; In-place partial edits.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 113 reference path: Metadata store separate from data nodes. → Erasure coding or 3 replicas across zones. → Multipart upload for large objects.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 113 risks: Durability: Eleven nines come from spreading fragments across failure domains and repairing faster than further failures occur; checksums catch silent corruption. Listing at scale: Prefix listing needs metadata sorted by key within a bucket, so the metadata store is range-partitioned by (bucket, key), with care for hot prefixes.

title: Distributed Counter
objectives: Scope Distributed Counter: increment a counter (likes, views), read the current count
Size it: 2B increments/day, about 120,000/s at peak
Defend the design: hot counters sharded into n sub-counters summed on read

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 114 · Distributed Counter: A distributed counter for likes and views that handles very hot counters. In scope: Increment a counter (likes, views); Read the current count; Handle very hot counters.

cards.title: Quality bar
cards.body: Boss 114 non-functionals: Increments under 10 ms. Counts may lag by a few seconds. No lost increments. Out of scope: Per-user like history UI; Fraud detection.

cards.title: Reference sketch
cards.body: Boss 114 reference path: Hot counters sharded into N sub-counters summed on read. → Increments batched by workers before hitting storage. → Consumers idempotent per event ID.

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 114 risks: No lost increments: Redis alone can lose recent writes on failover; the Kafka log or periodic durable snapshots allow counts to be rebuilt exactly. Lag versus cost: Summing 32 keys on every read is cheap with a short cache; allowing counts to lag a few seconds is what makes the design scale.

questions.prompt: Distributed Counter: assume 100M daily users each doing about 20 increments a day, with traffic peaking at 5× the daily average. Estimate peak increments per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 100M × 20 = 2B increments/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 23,000/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 120,000/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 100M × 20 = 2B increments/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 23,000/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 120,000/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A phone's like request times out and the app retries. How do you stop the like being counted twice?

choices.label: Raise the client timeout so retries never happen
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate
Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: A viral post gets 10× normal likes on one counter key with no sharding yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: One viral post's like counter is hammered by millions of increments. Which design choice is core to keeping it accurate and fast?

choices.label: Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low
Hot counters sharded into N sub-counters summed on read.
Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails

questions.explanation: Hot counters sharded into N sub-counters summed on read. Increments batched by workers before hitting storage. Consumers idempotent per event ID. The others are tempting but wrong: one big server is still a single point of failure, tight retry loops amplify an outage, and acknowledging before a durable write loses data on a crash.

questions.prompt: Distributed Counter must increment a counter (likes, views) while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?
constraints: Counts may lag by a few seconds

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

rationaleOptions.label: A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency
A queue removes the need to watch backlog
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request
User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.
